name: @bicharts/chart-mcp

tools.name: assess_data_shape
tools.description: Profile a dataset locally (no data leaves the machine): per-column types, cardinality, ranges, measure/dimension roles, temporal/ordinal detection, and cross-column signals (nesting, shared values, association). This is the same measurement engine the BIC Power BI visual uses before generating a chart.

csv_path.description: Path to a CSV file (header row required).

dataType.description: Known type (DAX/semantic-model callers have it); omit to infer from values.

isMeasure.description: Known measure/dimension role; omit to apply the numeric-non-identifier heuristic. A semantic-model caller should set this.

format.description: Format string from the model (e.g. "$#,##0") → modelFormat.

description.description: Column description from the model → modelDesc.

rows.description: Rows as positional arrays aligned to columns, OR objects keyed by column name.

data.description: A pre-typed {columns, rows} table — the shape a Fabric DAX query / dataframe already has. Alternative to csv_path/csv_text; when columns carry isMeasure/format/description the shape matches PBI fidelity with no guessing.

measures.description: Columns to treat as MEASURES (the PBI 'Values' well — fields the chart aggregates). Numeric non-identifier columns are measures by default.

dimensions.description: Columns to treat as DIMENSIONS (a PBI category/axis well — fields to group/break by). Use for numeric codes/years that should NOT be aggregated.

formats.description: Per-column number/date FORMAT STRING (e.g. {"Revenue":"$#,##0","Margin":"0.0%"}). PBI supplies these from its model; a CSV can't, so provide them to steer number formatting.

descriptions.description: Per-column human DESCRIPTION — gives the model semantic context the bare column name lacks.

group_by.description: Columns that are the PRIMARY series/breakdown (the PBI 'Group by' well); the backend leads the visualization with these.

non_additive.description: MEASURE columns that must NOT be summed (a ratio/average/rate — use mean, never stack). Usually auto-detected; this is an authoritative override.

privacy_level.description: How much detail to compute/share: 0 names only, 10 +counts, 20 +detailed stats (default), 30 +obfuscated sample rows.

culture.description: The caller's language and region as a BCP 47 tag such as 'de-DE', 'fr' or 'ja-JP'. Default 'en-US'. It is the language the chart's own text is written in (titles, axis labels, legends, notes), and it breaks the tie when a CSV's numbers or dates are ambiguous: 12.500 as twelve thousand five hundred or twelve and a half, 05.03.2024 as 5 March or 3 May. Set it from the end user's locale when you know it; it does not translate the data.

tools.name: get_guide
tools.description: How to build an app with these charts, from the guide this package ships. Local and free: no network, no credentials. topic 'fabric-app' (the default) is what a Microsoft Fabric App on the Rayfin data app template needs: what to pull, generating, wiring in React, the Fabric App section and the time-savers. 'all' is the whole guide, including Blazor. 'chart-shapes' lists every chart type with the columns, limits and renderers it needs.

tools.name: list_eligible_charts
tools.description: The AUTHORITATIVE list of chart types that can render this dataset — the server's own eligibility engine, NOT a local guess. Profiles the data locally, then sends that profile to the backend. NO LLM in the loop, but this is a NETWORK call and it is METERED — see the licensing note below. By default the tool DETECTS the project's language (JS/TS vs Python from the working dir) and returns the charts for THAT language, SCOPED and ordered by how well each type fits this data (best first; `order: 'variety'` favors newer and less-common types instead), each tagged with its source language and renderer. Pass `language` ('javascript'|'python') to force it, or `renderer` ('D3'/'PLOTLY'/…) to rank one specific renderer, or renderer '' for the full renderer-agnostic eligibility across ALL renderers (also ranked, by chart type alone, with no renderer/language tag). If the language can't be auto-detected and none is given, the tool asks you to specify one. Needs an account: eligibility IS the engine, so programmatic access to it is licensed. With nothing configured, the first call opens a browser sign-in, waits for it and then answers (a license key in the environment is the alternative for a machine with no browser). Free within a generous hourly allowance; beyond it each call draws usage credits. The reply carries a text block and a structured table: one row per chart type with its rank, name, preview flag, fit verdict, description, language and renderer. Rows flagged alsoWorthALook are a few picks from below the top fits, drawn so an offer can include something different; the fit order itself never changes.

language.description: Project source language → the server ranks across that language's renderers (javascript/typescript = D3/Vega, python = Plotly/matplotlib). Omit to AUTO-DETECT from the working dir; `renderer` (if given) overrides this.

project_dir.description: Directory to auto-detect the project language from (default: the folder setup_fabric_app used, else the working directory or the one project folder directly inside it).

renderer.description: Force a specific renderer (overrides `language`): a concrete renderer ranks that renderer's charts; '' = the full renderer-agnostic eligibility (all renderers, ranked by chart type alone). Omit to use `language`/auto-detection.

level_of_detail.description: The user's own preference for how much of the data to see, as they've stated it. 'High' = every observation as its own mark, 'Medium' = every row shown as a distribution, 'Low' = one mark per category. Ranks this list the same way a generation would. Unset when they haven't stated one; unset changes nothing.

name_filter.description: Show only chart types matching this text (the same matcher the Power BI and Excel chart-type lists use). Three tiers, first non-empty one wins outright: the term starting a WORD in the name ('gan' -> Gantt chart, and NOT Organization chart), then mid-word in the name ('eth' -> Choropleth), then the description. A name match therefore SUPPRESSES description matches. Case- and accent-insensitive and, by default, space- and punctuation-insensitive too ('barchart' and 'bar-chart' find Bar chart; see name_filter_match). Minimum two characters, and it never reorders - the picker's ranking is preserved and the ranks stay as issued. Applied after ranking and before `top`.

name_filter_match.description: How name_filter matches a name. 'loose' (the default) ignores accents, case, spaces and punctuation, so 'barchart' finds Bar chart. 'exact' folds accents and case and collapses repeated spaces, and nothing else: a name typed without its space or hyphen matches nothing. The same setting the Power BI and Excel chart-type lists offer.

order.description: How the list is ordered. 'fit' (the default) = by how well each chart type fits THIS data, nothing else - use it to choose a chart for a question. 'variety' = the picker's selection order, which favors newer and less-common types on purpose - use it when the user wants to explore or be surprised. Both lists hold the same chart types; only the order differs.

top.description: Show only the top-N ranked results. Omit for all.

width.description: Viewport width px (default 800) — affects small-viewport / facet-budget gates.

tools.name: generate_chart
tools.description: Generate ready-to-render chart code for a dataset via the BIC backend: the data shape is profiled locally, the backend picks a suitable chart type (or honors chart_type), and returns code that has passed the backend's eligibility gates and quality checks. Needs a trial or paid account: with nothing configured, the first call opens a browser sign-in, waits for it and then finishes the chart (a license key in the environment or ~/.bic/credentials.json is the alternative for a machine with no browser). The returned D3 code is a portable render(container, data, options) function meant to be MERGED into your own app; an integration contract describes exactly how to call it. A standalone HTML preview and file output are optional.

Set it from the end user's locale when you know it; it does not translate the data.

prompt.description: Freeform guidance for the generation — the same 'user commentary' lane the Power BI visual uses. Steer encoding/axes/emphasis in plain language, e.g. 'put Year on the x-axis, color by Division', 'render citations as a chord diagram', 'log scale on revenue', 'annotate the peak'.

chart_type.description: Preferred chart type by name (honored unless the data shape disqualifies it).

rows_policy.description: 'auto' (default) = the engine decides how to summarize. 'all' = render EXACTLY one mark/row per source row, with no Top-N, no 'Other' rollup and no sampling. Use 'all' when your app depends on every row being present (a row-per-entity table, a point per location).

required_columns.description: Fields that MUST be visible in the output, each as its own column/channel. AUTHORITATIVE and VERIFIED: if the generated code never references one, the server regenerates automatically rather than returning a chart that silently dropped it.

forbid_derived_columns.description: True = show only fields present in the data (plus required_columns) — no per-capita, share-of-total, index, rank or z-score columns the engine would otherwise add. Use when your app owns the analytics and the chart is only the display.

level_of_detail.description: The user's own preference for how much of the data to see, as they've stated it; it isn't a property of the data. 'High' = every observation drawn as its own mark (scatter, beeswarm, strip). 'Medium' = every row used, but shown as a distribution (box, violin, histogram). 'Low' = one mark per category (bars, cards, pies). Unset when the user hasn't stated one; unset is a proven no-op and the engine decides. This is a strong nudge, not a filter: it reorders charts that already fit, and an explicit chart_type still wins.

font_family.description: CSS font family for the chart's own text — titles, axis labels, tick labels, legends (e.g. 'Segoe UI' or a stack like 'Segoe UI, Arial, sans-serif'). Set ONLY when the user has named a font or stated a house style; a font isn't a property of the data or the project. Unset when none was given; unset is a proven no-op and the engine picks. Applies to whichever renderer is chosen (D3, Plotly, matplotlib and Vega each get an equivalent instruction), and an unavailable family falls back to a web-safe stack rather than failing.

renderer.description: Force a specific renderer (overrides `language`). Omit to use `language`/auto-detection; 'VISUAL'/'' = let the backend choose.

language.description: Project source language: with no concrete `renderer`, javascript/typescript generates D3 (the renderer @bicharts/chart-host draws) and python lets the backend auto-pick within Plotly/matplotlib. Omit to AUTO-DETECT from the working dir.

project_dir.description: Directory to auto-detect the project language from (default: the folder setup_fabric_app used, else the working directory or the one project folder directly inside it).

reasoning_mode.description: LLM pass structure; empty = backend heuristic.

wrap.description: Code form: 'none' (default) = the raw render() function to merge; 'esm' = same code plus `export { render };` so the file can be `import`ed. Both forms are accepted everywhere - @bicharts/chart-host strips the export clause before compiling - so this is a convenience, never a compatibility choice.

include_code.description: Include the full code in the response — governs BOTH the text block and structuredContent.code. Default: true, or FALSE when out_dir is given (the code is then already on disk, and a large chart's code can overflow a client's tool-output limit). Set it explicitly to override either default.

preview_html.description: Also emit a standalone D3 preview (needs out_dir). Default false — the code is meant to be merged, not run as an index.html.

out_dir.description: Optional directory to write chart.js/py, a data.sample.json, and (if preview_html) preview.html.

tools.name: preview_request
tools.description: Shows exactly what a chart generation would send to the BIC backend for these arguments - the measured shape of your data (column names, types, counts, ranges), the settings, and whether any sample rows travel - with the credentials removed. SENDS NOTHING and needs no license: it is local and free. Takes the same arguments as a generation. It answers 'what data leaves my machine?'; the eligibility list sends a subset of the same shape.

tools.name: check_chart
tools.description: Verify a generated chart locally before deploying: draws the chart.js that generate_chart wrote, headless, against its data - the rows query_semantic_model saved, a CSV, or the rows it was generated for - through @bicharts/chart-host the way the app will, and reports in plain words: the marks drawn by kind, anything thrown (with the line), whether it came out blank, anything drawn outside its frame, and whether a click on a mark reaches onSelect with source rows. Takes seconds; local and free (no network, no credentials, nothing sent). Run it after each generate_chart instead of deploying to see whether a chart works, and check at the size the panel will give it: by default it reads minChartWidth and minChartHeight off the app's BicChartPanel around the chart (else the size it was generated for); pass width and height only for another size. A WARNING line is a label cut off at that size even at a narrow font's width; the reply says whether more room fixes it. Never edit the generated chart code by hand to clear a finding: regenerate it (generate_chart, with a prompt describing the fix) or report it. It does not judge colours or real font widths.

chart.description: The chart's folder name under the project's src/charts (the out_dir given to generate_chart), e.g. "region-map".

chart_path.description: Or the path of the chart.js generate_chart wrote, or the folder it is in.

project_dir.description: The app's folder. Defaults to the folder setup_fabric_app used, else the working directory or the one project folder inside it.

data_name.description: The name given to query_semantic_model: checks on the rows it saved (.bic/data/<name>.csv). Default: a saved file named like the chart's folder, else the rows the chart was generated for.

csv_path.description: Or a CSV with the chart's columns.

width.description: The width in px to check at (default: the minChartWidth of the app's BicChartPanel around this chart, else the width it was generated for, else 800).

height.description: The height in px to check at (default: the minChartHeight of the app's BicChartPanel around this chart, else the height it was generated for, else 600).

tools.name: check_app
tools.description: Check how the app uses the chart library, before every deploy and after check_chart: reads the app's own source (never the files generate_chart and setup_fabric_app wrote) and reports, each with file, line and the library call to use instead: hand-written selection glue (a toggle, a second-click guard, a remount to clear) where useBicFilter + selects does it; row positions read from the DOM; the payload's __rowIdx__ / __geo* columns built by hand; a slider beside a chart that draws its own controls (useBicControls); notes kept but never shown on the marks (annotations); a chart outside a BicChartPanel, a fixed height below the panel's minimum, a flex-1 container without min-h-0 / min-w-0; two charts setting the same element id; and @bicharts / Rayfin / Fabric visuals packages behind npm's latest. It also draws every chart under src/charts the way check_chart does and reports any that throw, come out blank or don't pass a click to onSelect. Local and free; npm is only asked for versions, and a stack finding is skipped when npm can't be reached. Layout findings are WARNINGS: a static read can't prove a layout. Fix the app's own files; regenerate a chart rather than edit its generated code.

project_dir.description: The app's folder. Defaults to the folder setup_fabric_app used, else the working directory or the one project folder inside it.

draw_charts.description: Also draw every chart under src/charts (default true).

check_npm.description: Compare the stack with npm's latest (default true).

annotations.title: Check the whole app before deploying

tools.name: setup_fabric_app
tools.description: Run once in a Microsoft Fabric App scaffolded from Rayfin's data app template, before the first chart: installs @bicharts/chart-host (at this server's version) and d3, adds src/lib/bic-chart-options.ts (the app's Fabric theme as chart options) and src/components/bic-chart-panel.tsx (a chart box that measures itself and shows the query's loading, error and empty states) and .agents/skills/regiabi-charts/SKILL.md, ignores .bic/, and puts every @microsoft/rayfin-* package on npm's latest, the release `rayfin init` installs (run it before rayfin init; every package.json range it changes is listed, and the reply names the Rayfin version installed). Never overwrites a file; the one template file it edits - a vi.mock that fixes the template's own validate-visual test under ESM - is named in the reply, as is the one line of src/main.tsx it points at src/lib/bic-css-theme.ts (the theme without bundling Vega). With features: ["notes"] and/or ["scenarios"] (once Rayfin's data service is on), it also adds finished notes-on-marks and saved-scenario files - the Rayfin entities, registered in rayfin/data/schema.ts, a hook each, a notes dialog and a scenarios panel - built on chart-host's useBicFilter / useBicControls; write none of that by hand. Replies with a worked example that renders a generated chart from a live query.

project_dir.description: The Fabric App project folder. Defaults to the working directory, or the one Fabric App folder directly inside it.

skip_install.description: Add the files only; don't run npm install.

features.description: Also add finished files for readers' notes on chart marks ("notes") and saved settings of a chart's own controls ("scenarios", e.g. a What-if chart's rate). Needs Rayfin's data service on (rayfin/data/schema.ts); the reply says the command when it isn't. Never overwrites.

annotations.title: Set up a Fabric App for these charts

tools.name: query_semantic_model
tools.description: In a Microsoft Fabric App built on Rayfin's data app template: runs one chart's DAX query through the project's own `fabric-app-data` CLI, renames the `Table[Column]` and `[Measure]` headers to plain names (the names the chart.component.tsx that generate_chart writes will match on live rows), saves EVERY row as CSV, reads each column's role, format and description from the model, and profiles the result. Replaces the query, rename, save and profile steps with one call, and returns the arguments to pass to list_eligible_charts and generate_chart. Write the query at the chart's grain (one row per country for a country map). Local: the data goes only where the project's CLI already sends it, and nothing reaches the chart server.

dax.description: The chart's DAX query (EVALUATE ...). Or pass dax_file.

dax_file.description: Path to a .dax file holding the query, instead of dax.

name.description: A file name for this chart's data, e.g. "region-map" (saved as <name>.csv).

project_dir.description: The Fabric App project folder (holds fabric.yaml and node_modules). Defaults to the folder setup_fabric_app used, else the working directory or the one Fabric App folder directly inside it.

alias.description: The semantic model's alias in fabric.yaml. Needed only when the active profile has more than one.

out_dir.description: Where to save the CSV. Defaults to <project_dir>/.bic/data.

annotations.title: Query the semantic model for a chart

tools.name: suggest_charts
tools.description: Which charts suit this data? Answers 'what are good chart types for this dataset / model', 'what can I chart here', 'recommend some charts' for a semantic model in a Microsoft Fabric App built on Rayfin's data app template, in ONE call, from the model's real rows: reads its tables, columns, measures and relationships through the project's own `fabric-app-data` CLI, finds its natural views (measures by place, flows between places, measures over time, measures by category), queries each at its grain, keeps the measures that vary there, and asks the server's eligibility engine what fits each view. Replies view by view with the real counts (rows, places, periods, categories) and the chart types that fit, and saves each view's rows and DAX under .bic/data so generate_chart can build any of them next. Pass `views` to ask about your own groupings. Answer the person from this reply rather than from general knowledge. One eligibility call per view: metered like list_eligible_charts (free within an hourly allowance, usage credits beyond it) and needs the same licence. For one table you already hold, use list_eligible_charts.

name.description: A short name; the rows are saved as .bic/data/<name>.csv.

columns.description: The columns to group by, as Table[Column], e.g. ["Geography[Region]"].

measures.description: Measure names, e.g. ["Revenue"]. Omit to use the ones that vary most usefully at this grain.

dax.description: Or the view's own DAX query (EVALUATE ...), run as given.

views.description: Groupings to ask about instead of the model's own. Omit to let the model's structure decide.

top.description: How many fitting chart types to name per view (default 6).

project_dir.description: The Fabric App project folder (holds fabric.yaml and node_modules). Defaults to the folder setup_fabric_app used, else the working directory or the one Fabric App folder directly inside it.

alias.description: The semantic model's alias in fabric.yaml. Needed only when the active profile has more than one.

annotations.title: Suggest charts for a semantic model

instructions:
This is RegiaBI's chart server (npm @bicharts/chart-mcp); it builds charts from a table you hold. When a request asks for RegiaBI charts, it means these tools.
Starting to build an app with charts - a Microsoft Fabric App or any other? Your FIRST step, before you scaffold anything, is get_guide (topic 'fabric-app' for a Fabric App, else 'all'): it carries the scaffold command and the setup steps.
For a Fabric App over a semantic model, scaffold from Rayfin's dataapp template (npx -y @microsoft/create-rayfin --template dataapp), not blankapp; run setup_fabric_app once, then query_semantic_model runs a chart's DAX, saves every row and profiles it in ONE call.
Asked which charts suit the data? Answer from these tools, not from general knowledge: list_eligible_charts for a table you hold; over a Fabric App's semantic model, suggest_charts does it in ONE call, querying the model's natural views and returning what fits each.
Five rules for charts that fit on the first try:
1. Pass the chart's WHOLE result at its grain, not a sample: what fits depends on its counts. Use csv_path when long.
2. Give columns the plain names your app renders with (rename Table[Column] first), unchanged at render time.
3. To pick a type, call list_eligible_charts on that data first and choose what answers the question as asked. Pass chart_type only for a type the person named; else leave it unset and the engine chooses. Where a chart has controls drawn inside the chart, build no input beside it.
4. Host the code with @bicharts/chart-host. With out_dir, a D3 chart comes with chart.component.tsx beside chart.js, wired to generate_chart's binding: import it rather than writing one, and never hand-build __rowIdx__ or __geo* columns.
5. Use `prompt` for what the chart shows; selection, cross-filtering, sizing and theming are the host's: filter with useBicFilter + selects, read a chart's sliders with useBicControls + controls (@bicharts/chart-host/react). Never write a select handler, toggle or clear.
The guide is also skills/bic-charts/SKILL.md.
